constitutional_order.name: The Constitution of the Reckoning
constitutional_order.body: Drafted in eleven weeks between November 1992 and January 1993 and ratified in February on a 61% turnout, the constitution is a semi-presidential compromise. Baran's people, Doncic's people and the National Conservatives each held a veto. Its ambiguities are the price of getting it signed, not drafting oversights.

institutions.name: The National Assembly — the Chamber
institutions.body: One hundred seats and a four-year term: sixty by national list at a five per cent threshold, forty in single-member districts. List seats belong to parties; district seats belong to whoever controls the locality. Roughly a dozen district members are only nominally members of the colours under which they ran.

institutions.name: The Presidency
institutions.body: The directly elected President serves five years with a mandate separate from the Chamber and is not the player. The office commands the armed forces, appoints the senior prosecutor, security director and Chief of General Staff subject to confirmation, may return a bill once, and may call a consultative referendum. Article 61 permits measures necessary to preserve the constitutional order; neither the measures nor their limit are defined.

institutions.name: The Council of Ministers
institutions.body: The player is Chairman of the Council of Ministers — Prime Minister in everything but the Union-era title the constitution retained. The Chairman runs government, controls the budget, appoints ministers and requires the Chamber's confidence. The President is a rival mandate rather than an enemy, and cooperation with him is finite.

institutions.name: The Constitutional Court
institutions.body: Nine judges: three presidential nominees, three chosen by two-thirds of the Chamber, and three from the conference of senior judges, still dominated by Union-era appointees. It may strike a law on referral from the President, the government, or thirty Chamber members.

institutions.name: The National Bank of Ardenia
institutions.body: Statutorily independent since February 1993 as a condition of the first stabilisation agreement. It issues the kron and may not be instructed to finance the deficit. It may be pressured, and its independence may be repealed, but neither is costless.

institutions.name: The Prosecutor General's Office
institutions.body: The least reformed institution in Ardenia remains a Union-era procuracy with supervisory power over the administration and the ability to open a criminal file on any official. The appointment belongs to the President and can end careers.

institutions.name: The regional governors
institutions.body: Governors are appointed by the Council of Ministers under an emergency Baran-period arrangement provisionally preserved by the constitution. Whether organic law should make them elected is the largest unresolved constitutional question: Zavost might elect a Kolvenian regionalist, and Anera whoever Vasca blessed.

institutions.name: The Ardenian Army
institutions.body: About 28,000 personnel under the Defence Ministry, poorly equipped and carrying the institutional wound of losing the Vetrenka War. The President is commander-in-chief.

institutions.name: The National Guard
institutions.body: About 11,000 personnel under the Interior Ministry, better paid, formed out of the Turn of the Year and disproportionately recruited from Anera. It and the Army answer day to day to different ministers and ultimately to the President; neither has been asked which order it would follow if those authorities diverged.

institutions.name: The State Security Service — the Directorate
institutions.body: The service inherited the Union Third Directorate's building, officers and files: forty years of records naming who informed on whom. A 1991 moratorium sealed the archive and expires by its own terms in 1994. The Church is one reason opening it is dangerous.

officeholders.name: President Marek Stanik
officeholders.body: A constitutional lawyer and Kestrel Square survivor, elected at the Reckoning as the compromise nobody objected to. He holds no party card, enormous moral standing, and the unused language of Article 61.

officeholders.name: Chief Justice Vera Lostane
officeholders.body: Chief Justice of a court balanced among three appointing authorities and surrounded by a judiciary still full of Union-era careers.

officeholders.name: Governor Emil Grast
officeholders.body: Governor of the National Bank, custodian of the kron and of an independence clause on which foreign stabilisation money depends.

officeholders.name: Catholicos-Patriarch Meletian IV
officeholders.body: Head of the Ardenian Apostolic Church, consecrated bishop in 1979. His authority reaches Anera and the country's moral register; his Union-era advancement makes the Directorate files personal.

law_and_power.name: Law without enforcement
law_and_power.body: The judiciary is Union-era, underpaid by a factor of ten relative to what a case is worth, and unreformed. Enforcing a judgment is a commercial transaction in most regions and simply unavailable in Anera.

law_and_power.name: Licences, arrears and privatisation
law_and_power.body: Ardenian corruption is less a matter of envelopes than of deciding who gets an import licence, whose wage arrears the budget clears, and how a plant is valued when sold. All three levers sit with the government; every Chamber faction has clients asking that they move.

law_and_power.name: The five outside office
law_and_power.body: Informal power sits with Baran's credibility, Doncic's untested hold on the officer corps, Yeska's Falcons and coastal money, Meletian IV's moral authority in Anera, and the possibility that Vasca still holds a legitimacy claim older than the constitution.

media_and_civil_society.name: State Television
media_and_civil_society.body: Still the only nationwide broadcaster. Its director is appointed by the government, and its evening bulletin is the most valuable asset in Ardenian politics.

media_and_civil_society.name: Vestnik
media_and_civil_society.body: The old Union daily is owned by nobody who will say and remains reliably hostile to reform.

media_and_civil_society.name: The Ardenian Courier
media_and_civil_society.body: Small, liberal and chronically unpaid; read by everyone who matters and almost nobody who votes.

media_and_civil_society.name: The regional press
media_and_civil_society.body: Owned locally, which in practice means owned by whoever runs the locality.

media_and_civil_society.name: The Kestrel Committee
media_and_civil_society.body: The families of the 1989 dead are morally unassailable and dangerous for any government to cross.

media_and_civil_society.name: The Union of Ardenian Veterans
media_and_civil_society.body: Thirty thousand Vetrenka War veterans, unemployed and organised: the largest pool of men in the country who will appear in a square when told.

media_and_civil_society.name: The Zavost trade unions
media_and_civil_society.body: The industrial federation is the only labour organisation with the reach to close a region rather than issue a statement.

media_and_civil_society.name: The foreign-funded organisations
media_and_civil_society.body: A thin layer of civic organisations whose overseas funding is real and whom the National Conservatives already describe as an embassy project.
